title: Fee Drag, Explained: Why a 15% PMS Sometimes Beats a 20% One
author: IndiaFundSearch
seoTitle: Fee drag explained — why 15% PMS sometimes beats 20% PMS
seoDescription: A walk through how management, performance, brokerage, GST, and custody fees compound over a 10-year horizon — and why the headline-rate winner often loses on net.

children.text: Two PMS strategies. Strategy A delivers a 15% gross CAGR. Strategy B delivers 20% gross. Which one ends up with more of your money in 10 years? Almost everyone says B. Almost everyone is sometimes wrong.
Where the gap actually comes from

Strategy A charges 1.5% management with no performance fee. Strategy B charges 1% management plus 20% above an 8% hurdle. On a 20% gross return, Strategy B's manager earns roughly 1% management plus 2.4% performance — total 3.4% in headline fees. Add 0.5% brokerage drag, 18% GST on advisory fees, and a flat ₹25k custody, and net returns close fast.
Compounding turns small gaps into wide ones

On a ₹50 lakh investment over 10 years, Strategy A often nets between ₹1.85–1.95 Cr. Strategy B, despite the higher gross, can land between ₹1.95–2.10 Cr — but only if it actually delivers the 20%. If gross drops to 17%, B can underperform A.
The takeaway
Higher gross is not the same as higher net. Run the math before you allocate. Our Fee X-Ray calculator does it for any structure — try it with a real fund's actual fees, not the marketing summary.

title: What to Ask Before Allocating to a Long-Short AIF
author: IndiaFundSearch
seoTitle: Long-short AIF Cat III: what to ask before allocating
seoDescription: Five questions that separate a credible Cat III hedge-fund-style strategy from one selling beta in a complicated wrapper.

children.text: Long-short Category III AIFs are pitched as the antidote to public-market volatility. Many are; many are not. Five questions narrow the universe quickly.
1. What's the gross-vs-net leverage history?

A long-short fund running 150% gross / 50% net is making a different bet than one at 110/90. If the manager can't articulate the band their book lives in, they're either inexperienced or hiding something.
2. What's the worst single-day P&L since inception?
Drawdown over a year is one number. Single-day P&L tells you about position sizing, derivatives sophistication, and risk discipline. Ask for it. A serious manager will produce it.
3. How is performance fee calculated on negative years?
High-water mark or not? Catch-up clauses? An honest manager walks you through their PPM line by line. If you hear "don't worry about that", worry.
4. Who's the prime broker?
Operational quality matters more in long-short than in long-only. The PB you can't pronounce is rarely the right answer.
5. What does this fund do that public markets can't?

If the answer is "go anywhere" or "we time the market", run. The strongest Cat III managers can articulate a specific, repeatable edge — sector spreads, M&A arb, structural inefficiencies in derivatives, etc. Vagueness is a red flag.

children.text: Editor's note: Ask the Manager is our standing series — recorded Q&As with the people actually running PMS, AIF and GIFT City strategies. Same six questions every issue. Different manager every time. No PR fluff, no marketing slides. The full audio sits at the bottom; the highlights below are lightly edited for length.
IFS · Q1 — What does the next decade of Indian compounders look like that the last one didn't?

"The lowest-hanging fruit — branded consumption, basic financial services — has been picked. The next decade rewards three categories: (i) sub-segment leaders in fragmented manufacturing categories, (ii) IT services moving up the value chain into product, and (iii) financialisation plays beyond AMC and bank — exchanges, custodians, depositories. The names that worked from 2014–2024 won't be the same names that work from 2024–2034."
IFS · Q2 — What's a stock you bought after a 25%+ drawdown that taught you something?

"I'll tell you the one we sold during the drawdown and regretted. We exited a quality auto-ancillary in 2020 because we thought EV transition would crush them. They pivoted to EV components and tripled in three years. The lesson: capable managements pivot faster than your model assumes. Don't exit on macro narrative when the underlying capital allocator has a 20-year track record."
IFS · Q3 — Fee structure: what's fair, in your view?

"Honest answer? The 1.5% + 15% over 10% hurdle is fair when the manager genuinely earns the alpha. It's not fair when the manager is closet-tracking. We've resisted moving to performance-only despite client pressure because performance fees can incentivise concentration risk we wouldn't otherwise take. Fixed fees keep us aligned. That said, no fund — including ours — should charge a performance fee without a high-water mark."
IFS · Q4 — Where do you think most retail HNIs misallocate?

"Concentration in PMS at the wrong portfolio stage. A first-time HNI with ₹2 Cr and no prior equity exposure should not allocate ₹50L to a single concentrated PMS. Build the equity-mutual-fund layer first. Once the base portfolio has weathered a real drawdown — not a paper drawdown — then add concentrated PMS. The ₹50L minimum is a regulatory floor, not a starting point."
IFS · Q5 — What public data do you wish more investors looked at?

"Annual reports — not the chairman's letter. The schedule of receivables and payables, related-party transactions, and the cash-flow reconciliation. If a company's reported profit and operating cash flow have diverged for three years running, the profit is a story the auditors are letting them tell. SEBI doesn't flag this; you have to read it."
IFS · Q6 — What's the question you wish more investors asked you?

"'When would you sell?' Most clients ask about buying. The harder discipline is the sell rule. Ours is binary: if our investment thesis on a name fundamentally changes — capital allocation deteriorates, governance shifts, the business model the company writes down stops being the one they execute — we exit, regardless of what the price has done. About a third of our turnover comes from this rule, and it's the third we're proudest of."
Methodology

Ask the Manager is recorded over 30–40 minutes; ~70% of the transcript is published, lightly edited for length and clarity. We send the manager every quote before publication and accept factual corrections only — not editorial revisions. The series is unsponsored. Managers are selected based on AUM scale and SEBI / IFSCA registration; we do not accept fees, gifts, or paid placements.
